planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in deep, reliably moist, fertile soil in partial shade with shelter from drying wind; Siberian ligularia wilts on bright, windy days even when soil moisture is adequate, so a sheltered, waterside site suits it best.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in deep, moderately fertile, reliably moist soil in partial shade, choosing a site sheltered from strong wind since exposed plants wilt visibly on bright, breezy days regardless of soil moisture. Siberian ligularia forms a tidy clump of rounded, toothed, heart-shaped leaves considerably smaller and less coarse than those of Ligularia dentata, giving it a more refined, less tropical look in the border. From midsummer into early fall, branched racemes of small, bright yellow daisy flowers rise on slender dark stems above the foliage, opening in a looser, airier arrangement than the dense spikes of stenocephala types. It is an excellent choice for a streamside or pond-margin planting where its native Eurasian wetland habit can be echoed, and it divides readily every few years in spring to maintain vigor.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in deep, moist to boggy, humus-rich, fertile soil in partial shade; Hodgson's ligularia is a compact relative of Ligularia dentata that suits a smaller moist shade bed than the larger bigleaf cultivars.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in deep, moist to boggy, fertile, humus-rich soil in partial shade, keeping the root zone from drying out through the growing season. Hodgson's ligularia forms a dense, low clump of thick, rounded, dark green leaves markedly more compact than Ligularia dentata, to which it is closely related, making it a good choice for a smaller moist shade border or the front of a pond-edge planting. In late summer into early fall, clusters of orange-yellow daisy flowers open on stems held just above the foliage mound. Native to stream banks, grassy slopes, and forest margins from far eastern Russia and China to Japan and northern Vietnam, it wants the same reliably damp, humus-rich conditions as its larger cousins and divides easily in spring every few years to renew the clump.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in deep, reliably moist, fertile soil in partial shade with shelter from strong wind; Zepter is a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit ligularia grown for its tall, dark-stemmed flower spires.

directions: Plant divisions in spring in deep, moderately fertile, reliably moist soil in partial shade with some relief from midday sun, and shelter the site from strong wind. Zepter bears large, heart-shaped, toothed mid-green leaves in a bold basal clump, and in late summer sends up tall wand-like spires of black-purple stems studded with spidery yellow-orange flowers that open in sequence from the base upward, giving a long season of vertical color well above the foliage. Named for the German word for scepter and holder of a Royal Horticultural Society Award of Garden Merit, it is a dramatic architectural accent for a bog garden or pond margin where its considerable thirst for moisture can be reliably met. Divide congested clumps in early spring every few years to maintain vigor.
